     3	date: 2026-09-08
     4	decision-makers: [adss maintainers]
     5	slice: 3
     6	---
     7	
     8	# A measure is owned by an event and named for an entity, so two events on one entity may not name the same measure
     9	
    10	## Context and Problem Statement
    11	
    12	Slice 3 is the first slice where one entity has two events: an order is both placed and shipped.
    13	That splits two things which have been the same thing until now.
    14	
    15	A measure's **column** and its **glossary token** are keyed on the entity:
    16	
    17	```python
    18	(event, measure, f"_measure__{event.entity_id.lower()}__{measure.id.lower()}")
    19	found[f"{event.entity_id}.measures.{measure.id}"] = measure.definition
    20	```
    21	
    22	Its **ownership** is keyed on the event — `_branch` decides which stage carries a value and which
    23	emits a typed null by identity on the event object. So the generator knows exactly which stage owns
    24	a measure, and then names it after something else.
    25	
    26	With one event per entity those keys coincide and nothing can go wrong. With two, declaring the
    27	same measure id on both events of one entity is accepted without a word, and produces:
    28	
    29	- **the same column twice** in the published contract, and
    30	- **one definition silently replacing the other** in the glossary.
    31	
    32	Reproduced on the neutral fixture. The column list came back with
    33	`_measure__parent__happened_parents_count` at two positions, and the glossary held the *second*
    34	event's definition under the first event's token.
    35	
    36	The two halves fail very differently. DuckDB does not refuse two columns of one name — measured,
    37	`CREATE TABLE t AS SELECT 1 AS a, 2 AS a` yields `a` and `a_1` — so the built table's columns would
    38	not match `bridge_columns()` and the contract check would fail the build loudly. That half is safe.
    39	
    40	**The glossary half is caught by nothing.** No check inspects `definitions()`. That dictionary is
    41	what a question's `defines` entries are resolved against, and what the page renders as "What the
    42	words mean". So a question could reference a measure, resolve it successfully, and be shown a
    43	definition belonging to a different measure — on the page a reader accepts the slice on — while
    44	every test and every check passes.
    45	
    46	Nothing enforces the naming convention that would prevent it either. Conventions §2's three-part
    47	pattern is a hard rule, and there is no test anywhere that checks a measure name's shape. The
    48	uniqueness of these columns has rested entirely on a rule enforced by reading.
    49	
    50	## Decision Drivers
    51	
    52	* a definition that is silently replaced is worse than one that is missing: nothing looks wrong
    53	* the failure must be loud where it is invisible, not only where DuckDB happens to complain
    54	* a published column contract two consumers are already written against
    55	* whatever is decided now is cheapest now, with two questions in existence
    56	
    57	## Considered Options
    58	
    59	* Refuse the collision when the declarations are read, and keep the entity in the column name
    60	* Rename the column to `_measure__<event>__<measure>` and the token to `<ENTITY>.<EVENT>.measures.<M>`
    61	* Do nothing, and rely on §2's naming pattern to keep ids distinct
    62	
    63	## Decision Outcome
    64	
    65	Chosen: **refuse the collision when the declarations are read.**
    66	
    67	Two events on one entity may not declare the same measure id. The refusal names both events and
    68	says what would be lost, because the loss is not obvious: a reader who has just been told the
    69	column would be duplicated will think of the column, and the definition is the part nothing else
    70	would catch.
    71	
    72	**Why not rename to the event.** It is more correct in principle — the event is what actually owns
    73	a measure, so the name should say so — and it is the cheapest it will ever be, with only two
    74	questions to update. It is rejected on two counts. It changes a published contract that conventions
    75	§1.3 states as a hard rule and ADR 0002 tabulates, in a slice that has no other reason to touch it.
    76	And §2's descriptor slot already carries the event: `placed_orders_count`, `shipped_orders_count`.
    77	Naming the column for the event too would put it in twice, so the more correct scheme reads worse
    78	in every ordinary case in order to disambiguate one that is now refused outright.
    79	
    80	**Why not do nothing.** §2's pattern makes a collision unlikely, not impossible, and "unlikely" is
    81	the wrong guarantee for a failure whose signature is a page showing a plausible sentence about the
    82	wrong number. Two events on one entity is exactly where the pattern's descriptor slot stops doing
    83	the work — `placed` and `shipped` distinguish the count measures, and nothing forces a third
    84	measure to carry a descriptor at all.
    85	
    86	This follows the shape the repository already uses for the same class of problem: ADR 0006 refuses
    87	two edges that would inherit into one key column, for the same reason and with the same argument
    88	about what DuckDB silently does instead of raising. A generator that cannot emit a correct artefact
    89	should say so rather than emit an ambiguous one.
    90	
    91	## Consequences
    92	
    93	* Good, because the glossary can no longer show one measure's definition under another's name,
    94	  which was the only failure here that nothing would have reported
    95	* Good, because it is a refusal in the same place and the same shape as the one for colliding
    96	  edges, so the two read as one rule rather than two special cases
    97	* Good, because it costs nothing today: no existing declaration collides, and no column moves
    98	* Bad, because it forbids a legitimate-sounding declaration — the same quantity measured at two
    99	  events, deliberately, under one name. That would have to be two measures with two definitions,
   100	  which is more honest but more typing. If a slice ever wants it, the answer is to rename to the
   101	  event, and this record is what it supersedes
   102	* Bad, because the deeper mismatch stays: the generator still names by entity what it owns by
   103	  event. This narrows the consequence to nothing rather than removing the cause
   104	
   105	### A correction to ADR 0002
   106	
   107	The same mismatch makes one sentence of ADR 0002's published column contract false, for the first
   108	time, in this slice. `_stage` is defined there as "the entity this row is a row *of*", and
   109	`_measure__<entity>__<measure>` is described as "non-null only on the owning stage". With two
   110	events on `ORDER` both branches emit `_stage = 'order'`, so all 809 shipped rows share a stage with
   111	the placed rows while carrying a null `_measure__order__placed_orders_count`. The column is
   112	non-null only on the owning **event**, which `_event` names and `_stage` does not. The contract's
   113	behaviour is right; that sentence describing it is not.
   114	
   115	## Confirmation
   116	
   117	`tests/test_uss.py` asserts that two events on one entity declaring one measure id are refused,
   118	and that the same id on two *different* entities is still accepted — which is the case the
   119	refusal must not catch, since `_measure__<entity>__` already distinguishes those.
   120	
   121	A second test asserts that `definitions()` returns one entry per declared measure, counting what
   122	the glossary returns rather than the declarations twice, so a silent overwrite fails on the count
   123	rather than on somebody reading a page carefully. That is the assertion that would have caught
   124	this, and it did not exist.
   125	
   126	Both of these were written wrong the first time and a review caught them, which is worth leaving in
   127	the record: the first named an acceptance case no fixture contained, and the second compared a list
   128	with itself. A Confirmation section that names a test is only as good as what the test actually
   129	constructs, and neither of these could have failed for the reason it was written down for.

=============== docs/adr/0009-a-stage-may-be-dated-by-a-date-it-inherits.md

     2	status: accepted
     3	date: 2026-09-08
     4	decision-makers: [adss maintainers]
     5	slice: 4
     6	---
     7	
     8	# A stage may be dated by a date it inherits along the walk, named where it is inherited from
     9	
    10	## Context and Problem Statement
    11	
    12	Slice 4 asks for revenue per order **month**. Revenue is measured on an order line — quantity
    13	times price less discount — so the bridge needs a row per line. And **an order line has no
    14	date.** The source's `OrderDetail` has five properties and not one of them is a date; the live
    15	`$metadata` says so, and there is nothing to map from.
    16	
    17	The generator can only date a stage by an attribute of the event's own entity. `read_uss`
    18	resolves `date_attribute` against `model.entity(event.entity_id)`, so naming the order's date on
    19	a line event fails with a bare `KeyError: "ORDER_LINE has no attribute 'PLACED_ON'"` — not even a
    20	`UssError`, so the refusal arrives with no explanation attached.
    21	
    22	Nor may any layer go and fetch one. M1 forbids a join or a subquery in a mapping's `table:`; M5
    23	forbids a reach into another table; a DAS contract has no key for a join. A second mapped table
    24	on `ORDER_LINE` would be keyed by the order, which is not a line.
    25	
    26	So the question the plan wrote down for this slice cannot be built at all without deciding
    27	something the plan did not anticipate.
    28	
    29	**What is already true, and is the whole reason this is small.** The walk exists. For every
    30	edge, `_inherit_cte` already resolves the parent **as of the observation time of the row that
    31	inherits** and puts the parent's key on the child's bridge row. ADR 0006 spent its whole decision
    32	on getting that instant right. A date is another column of the row the walk already found.
    33	
    34	This is also what a Unified Star Schema does. Puppini's bridge is a row per measurement event;
    35	the event for an order line is the order being placed, on the day it was placed. Dating a line by
    36	its order's date is not an accommodation — it is what the shape means.
    37	
    38	## Decision Drivers
    39	
    40	* the question is answerable at all, which today it is not
    41	* a bridge row is true as of one instant, and every column on it is true as of that same instant
    42	* a mechanism that already exists, extended, rather than a second one beside it
    43	* the date a reader sees is traceable to a definition in the one place data is explained
    44	* slice 5 walks two hops, and must not need a third mechanism
    45	
    46	## Considered Options
    47	
    48	* **(a)** The date inherits along the walk, named as `<ENTITY>.<ATTRIBUTE>` in the sidecar
    49	* **(b)** Record `OrderDetails?$expand=Order` so the landed line carries the order's date
    50	* **(c)** Give `ORDER_LINE` its own date attribute, mapped from the order via the source
    51	* **(d)** Drop the calendar and let the question group on the order peripheral's date
    52	
    53	## Decision Outcome
    54	
    55	Chosen: **(a), the date inherits along the walk**, written in `dab/uss.yaml` as
    56	
    57	```yaml
    58	    - id: ORDERED
    59	      entity: ORDER_LINE
    60	      date_attribute: ORDER.PLACED_ON      # qualified: inherited along the edge to ORDER
    61	```
    62	
    63	An unqualified `date_attribute` still means an attribute of the event's own entity, which is
    64	every event declared so far and stays the ordinary case. A qualified one names the entity the
    65	date is inherited from, and that entity must be reachable along a declared edge from the event's
    66	entity — otherwise it is refused, by name, with the edges that do exist listed.
    67	
    68	The date is resolved **in the same CTE and at the same instant as the key**, because they are the
    69	same row of the same parent. Anything else would put two instants on one bridge row, which is the
    70	confusion ADR 0006 calls the entire difference between the option it chose and the one it
    71	rejected. A line whose order cannot be resolved gets a null date and therefore no bridge row, by
    72	the filter the generator already emits — consistent with how an event that did not happen is
    73	already handled.
    74	
    75	**Why not (b), expanding the source record.** It is the cheap-looking one and it is the worst.
    76	`PLACED_ON` would then have two homes — the order's own attribute and a copy on every line — and
    77	B8 says a definition exists exactly once. Two homes is how two reports start disagreeing, and
    78	this one would disagree *silently*, because both copies come from the same load and would agree
    79	until the first time they did not. It also needs a new contract key and a new `Endpoint` field to
    80	build a URL the recorder cannot currently express.
    81	
    82	**Why not (c), a mapped date on the line.** Same objection with an extra step: the mapping would
    83	have to reach into another table to get it, which M5 forbids outright.
    84	
    85	**Why not (d), grouping on the peripheral.** The stage still needs a non-null date to exist at
    86	all, so it does not escape the problem. And ADR 0007 rejected the peripheral-as-of-now reasoning
    87	already: a peripheral is current state, a bridge row is the version in which the event is dated,
    88	and reading one against the other puts two instants on one answer.
    89	
    90	### What this does not become
    91	
    92	The temptation this record exists to close is to let `date_attribute` take an expression, or to
    93	let it reach further than one declared edge because "the walk goes there anyway". Neither. The
    94	value is *a date attribute of an entity reached along a declared edge*, resolved exactly as its
    95	key is resolved. Arithmetic on it belongs in the mapping under ADR 0007; anything else is a
    96	second expression language in a file that is not linted, which ADR 0007 refused on §3.
    97	
    98	## Consequences
    99	
   100	* Good, because the question is answerable, and answerable at the grain it is asked at
   101	* Good, because it reuses the walk rather than adding a mechanism beside it: one more column off
   102	  a row the generator already resolves, at an instant it already got right
   103	* Good, because slice 5's two-hop chain inherits this unchanged — a date reached along two edges
   104	  is the same rule applied twice, and needs no new decision
   105	* Good, because the date on a line is traceable to `ORDER.PLACED_ON`, which has one definition,
   106	  so the page's glossary can explain the axis a reader is looking at
   107	* Bad, because `dab/uss.yaml` now has two shapes for one field, and a reader has to know that a
   108	  dot means "inherited". The alternative — always qualifying — would rewrite three existing
   109	  declarations for no gain, and `<ENTITY>.<ATTRIBUTE>` is the notation the questions already use
   110	* Bad, because a line's date now moves if its order is re-pointed to a different order, which
   111	  cannot happen in this source and is a real property of the design rather than a bug. The
   112	  as-of resolution is what bounds it: the date is the one in force when the line was observed
   113	
   114	## Confirmation
   115	
   116	`tests/test_uss.py` asserts that a qualified `date_attribute` is resolved from the inherited
   117	entity and not from the event's own; that it is refused, naming the available edges, when the
   118	entity it names is not reachable along one; that an unqualified one still means the event's own
   119	entity; and that the date and the key come from the same CTE, so no bridge row can carry two
   120	instants. A sidecar beside the neutral fixture gains an event on `CHILD` dated by
   121	`PARENT.HAPPENED_ON`, which is
   122	the shape this record is about and which the fixture did not have. Its SQL is linted with every
   123	other emitter's and executed by `tests/test_inherited_date_sql.py`, which builds a parent with
   124	more than one version -- the real warehouse has exactly one per key, so the real warehouse
   125	could not have shown either of the two defects that test was written for.
   126	
   127	A generated data check asserts that every bridge row of such a stage carries the same
   128	`_event_date` as the stage that **owns** that date, for the key on that row — 2,155 comparisons on
   129	the real build. It is independent rather than circular: the parent's own stage gets the date from
   130	its version CTE and the child's from its inherit CTE, so resolving the date at a different instant
   131	than the key, or against a different version of the parent, shows up here. Both of those are
   132	invisible in the warehouse otherwise. `tests/test_inherited_date_check.py` runs it against a
   133	bridge built to fail it.
   134	
   135	A check is generated only where the entity the date comes from has an event on that same
   136	attribute. Without one there is nothing independent to compare against, and a check that
   137	re-derives what it expects from the generator agrees with a broken generator.
   138	
   139	**This section previously claimed that check existed.** It did not: nothing in `src/adss/checks.py`
   140	emitted it and no such file was in `checks/`. A security review found the claim, and it is the
   141	third confirmation in this repository to name a check that could not do what it said — which is
   142	why the rule about running the mutation before writing the sentence now lives in the adss skill.
   143	
   144	What is **not** confirmed, and is recorded rather than claimed: a row dropped because its
   145	inherited date did not resolve. This decision makes such a row absent by construction, and an
   146	absent row disagrees with nothing. Checking that would need a count of the rows a stage *should*
   147	have, and nothing in the model states one — a line whose order has no date is legitimately absent,
   148	and no check can tell that from a line the generator lost.
=============== docs/adr/0010-a-composite-source-key-becomes-one-key-and-is-checked-against-its-parts.md
     1	---
     2	status: accepted
     3	date: 2026-09-08
     4	decision-makers: [adss maintainers]
     5	slice: 4
     6	---
     7	
     8	# A composite source key becomes one key expression, and a check compares it against the parts it was made from
     9	
    10	## Context and Problem Statement
    11	
    12	The source's order lines are keyed on `(OrderId, ProductId)`. Conventions M2 has permitted
    13	"a `concat` of casts with a separator" since slice 1 and warned that a concat without one makes
    14	`'A1' + '23'` and `'A12' + '3'` the same key — a clause that has been **review-only for three
    15	slices** because nothing had a composite key. This is the slice that has one.
    16	
    17	A probe built the whole slice four times over and measured what the rule has been asserting.
    18	
    19	**The collision this data can produce: none.** Over all 2155 real order lines, a separator-less
    20	concat yields 2155 distinct keys — because every `OrderId` is exactly five digits, so the split
    21	point is never ambiguous. A separator-less key would pass every gate, every data check and both
    22	acceptance queries. The warning is right in general and unfalsifiable here, which is the most
    23	dangerous shape a rule can have: it looks satisfied whatever you do.
    24	
    25	**A separator that can occur in a value does not fix it.** Measured, with `'-'` between
    26	`('A-1','23')` and `('A','1-23')`: five distinct keys from six pairs. With a separator outside
    27	the value domain: six from six. So "the parts are integers, so `-` is fine" is exactly the
    28	reasoning that is *fine today and wrong at the first string key* — and the key cannot be changed
    29	later, so "wrong later" means wrong with the old key already immortal.
    30	
    31	**`concat` ignores nulls; `||` does not.** Measured: `concat('1213','-',NULL)` is `'1213-'`, not
    32	null. `concat_ws` drops the separator too. `'1213' || '-' || NULL` is null. The source's metadata
    33	does **not** mark `OrderDetail.OrderId` or `ProductId` `Nullable="false"` — unlike `Order.OrderId`,
    34	which it does — so a null half silently produces a truncated key that collides with a real one.
    35	
    36	**M2's stated reason is wrong, and the truth is worse in a different way.** M2 says two entries
    37	are read as alternate identifiers and "that mode cannot be undone once loaded". Measured: two
    38	entries are **refused at deploy**, loudly, unless `allow_multiple_identifiers` is set on the
    39	mapping group. With it set, the entity key becomes a **minted UUID** — not derived from anything
    40	in DAS — so the layer stops being rebuildable from the source, which is a blueprint promise. The
    41	repository already catches that, but under the `_focal`/`_idfr` vendor pins, which name the
    42	wrong cause.
    43	
    44	**And the key expression genuinely cannot be changed after loading.** Changing only `'-'` to
    45	`'/'` and re-executing doubled everything: 2155 keys became 4310, and revenue over the bridge
    46	went from 1,265,793.0395 to 2,531,586.079. `adss check` caught it — as
    47	`ORDER_LINE_desc holds no duplicate versions … a growing gap is FULL ingestion duplicating
    48	silently`, which names a cause that has nothing to do with what happened and would cost a reader
    49	an afternoon.
    50	
    51	## Decision Drivers
    52	
    53	* a key that cannot collide, demonstrated rather than argued from the shape of the data
    54	* a rule that still holds when a later composite key has a string part
    55	* failing closed on a null part, rather than producing a shorter key that collides
    56	* the next person is told the truth about what two entries actually do
    57	
    58	## Considered Options
    59	
    60	* `concat` of casts with a separator — what M2's text suggests
    61	* `||` of casts with a separator, plus a check comparing the composed key against its parts
    62	* Two `primary_keys` entries with `allow_multiple_identifiers`
    63	* A surrogate minted in DAS
    64	
    65	## Decision Outcome
    66	
    67	Chosen: **`||` of casts with a separator, and a generated check that the composed key has exactly
    68	as many distinct values as the source's own composite key.**
    69	
    70	```yaml
    71	primary_keys: ["cast(order_id AS VARCHAR) || '-' || cast(product_id AS VARCHAR)"]
    72	```
    73	
    74	The check is the part that matters, and it is what turns three slices of asserted reasoning into
    75	something falsifiable. Whatever separator is chosen and whatever the parts turn out to be, the
    76	composed key must not collapse two source rows into one — and that is directly countable against
    77	the contract's own `primary_keys`, which DAS already records as a composite. A separator argument
    78	is a prediction; this is a measurement, and it fires on the data that actually landed.
    79	
    80	`||` rather than `concat`, because `concat` is null-blind: it turns a missing half into a shorter
    81	key that can collide with a real one, silently. `||` yields null, and a null key fails at the
    82	engine rather than in a report six months later. The dab skill recommends `concat`; that
    83	recommendation is wrong for a composite key and is corrected.
    84	
    85	**Why not two entries.** Not because M2's stated reason is right — it is not — but because what
    86	actually happens is worse: the entity key becomes a minted UUID with nothing in DAS to recompute
    87	it from, so DAB stops being rebuildable from the source. M2's text is corrected to say what the
    88	engine really does.
    89	
    90	**Why not a surrogate in DAS.** It would be minted there instead, with the same rebuildability
    91	problem one layer earlier, and DAS's job is to record what a source sent rather than to invent an
    92	identifier it did not.
    93	
    94	### On the separator, honestly
    95	
    96	`'-'` is chosen for readability — `10248-11` is a key a person can recognise in a screenshot —
    97	and it is safe here only because both parts are non-negative integers. That is not a general
    98	guarantee and this record does not pretend it is. **A composite key with a part that is not a
    99	non-negative integer is a new decision**, not an application of this one: the separator has to be
   100	chosen against that part's value domain, and the check below is what would catch a wrong choice.
   101	
   102	## Consequences
   103	
   104	* Good, because the property M2 has asserted for three slices is now measured on every build,
   105	  against the source's own key rather than against an argument about digits
   106	* Good, because a null part fails rather than producing a key that is quietly one character short
   107	* Good, because the check is generated per contract, so a later composite key is checked without
   108	  anything else changing
   109	* Bad, because the key is not a number the business uses. `10248-11` is this system's identifier
   110	  for a line, and no order form has ever carried it. If a question ever needs "which product", the
   111	  answer is a `PRODUCT` peripheral reached along an edge — slice 5's content — and **never**
   112	  splitting this string back apart, which would be a reach into a key's internals from a layer
   113	  that must not know it has any
   114	* Bad, because re-keying an entity after it is loaded doubles its history, and the check that
   115	  notices names the wrong cause. That is recorded here and left alone: the right repair is to drop
   116	  the schemas and rebuild, which the build already supports, and a check that explained it
   117	  properly would have to know what a re-key looks like
   118	
   119	## Confirmation
   120	
   121	`tests/test_mapping_rules.py` asserts that a composed key expression conforms to M2 — one entry,
   122	producing a VARCHAR — and that two entries are still refused before the engine sees them.
   123	
   124	A generated data check, one per contract with a composite key, counts the distinct composed keys
   125	in `das__staged.<table>__current` against the distinct source key tuples and fails on any
   126	difference. It is written against the shape that would break it — a separator-less concat over
   127	parts whose lengths vary — and that case is constructed in `tests/` so the check is known to be
   128	capable of failing, rather than known to pass.
   129	
   130	What is **not** confirmed, and is recorded rather than claimed: nothing detects that a key
   131	expression has *changed* between builds. The signature is a doubling of the description table,
   132	which an existing check reports under a name that describes a different defect. Making that
   133	check name the right cause would mean teaching it what a re-key looks like, and the repair — drop
   134	and rebuild — is the same either way.

     2	status: accepted
     3	date: 2026-09-08
     4	decision-makers: [adss maintainers]
     5	slice: 4
     6	---
     7	
     8	# A float in the source is recorded as a decimal, because the choice is about where a bad value fails
     9	
    10	## Context and Problem Statement
    11	
    12	`OrderDetail.Discount` is `Edm.Single` — a 32-bit float, and the first one this system has met.
    13	Revenue is quantity times unit price less that discount, so it feeds a measure.
    14	
    15	The contract vocabulary has `DOUBLE` and `DECIMAL` and no `REAL`. So **neither option is a
    16	transcription of what the source declares**; both are a choice, and §1.1's usual instruction —
    17	record what the source sent — does not settle it.
    18	
    19	ADR 0007 established that a question's two answers are compared row by row **by value**, and that
    20	a float makes that comparison order-dependent because summing doubles is not associative. Slice 4
    21	is the first slice that could actually trip it, so the question is whether it does.
    22	
    23	A probe built the slice twice, once with each type, and measured.
    24	
    25	**On this data, the two builds are indistinguishable.** Every DAR value byte-identical; zero of
    26	2155 revenue rows differ; both acceptance queries agree either way. Revenue uses at most four
    27	decimal places and `DECIMAL(28,8)` holds it with four to spare.
    28	
    29	**Not indistinguishable in general.** At a larger magnitude the same expression diverges:
    30	`97 * 1234567.8901 * (1 - 0.06)` is `112567900.21931798` through a double and
    31	`112567900.21931800` through a decimal.
    32	
    33	**And the order-dependence ADR 0007 predicted is live on this slice's own measure.** Summing the
    34	2155 real revenue values as doubles, in three different orders:
    35	
    36	```
    37	ORDER BY order_id, product_id            -> 1265793.0395000004
    38	ORDER BY product_id DESC, order_id DESC  -> 1265793.0394999993
    39	ORDER BY unit_price, quantity            -> 1265793.0395000007
    40	```
    41	
    42	Three orders, three answers. ADR 0007 wrote that down as a prediction; this is the witness.
    43	
    44	**Where the float actually stops, and who stops it.** At `dab.<E>_desc.val_num`, a
    45	`DECIMAL(28,8)` column the engine coerces into silently. Every presentation object gives
    46	`DECIMAL(28,8)` whatever DAS declared. **Nobody in this repository wrote that cast and nothing
    47	names it** — which means the answer side of every question is protected by a vendor's choice
    48	rather than by ours.
    49	
    50	**The exactness check added in slice 3 is silent here**, and it is worth being exact about why.
    51	It inspects returned values, and both sides launder the float before it sees them: the answer
    52	side is `DECIMAL(28,8)` because DAB widens every `NUMBER`, and every control query already wraps
    53	its sum in a cast. Measured: with a `DOUBLE` contract the check reports nothing — unless the
    54	question's author omits that cast, in which case it fires. So it defends against a float in an
    55	*answer*, not against a float in a *source*, and slice 4 was expected to trip it and does not.
    56	
    57	## Decision Drivers
    58	
    59	* a bad value fails where somebody can see it, rather than propagating
    60	* the exactness the acceptance check depends on does not rest on a vendor's silent coercion
    61	* §1.1 keeps DAS a recording, so a type is chosen for how it fails, not for what it computes
    62	* the choice survives a source whose values are larger than this one's
    63	
    64	## Considered Options
    65	
    66	* `DOUBLE` — closest to what `Edm.Single` is
    67	* `DECIMAL(18, 4)` — what the values actually are
    68	
    69	## Decision Outcome
    70	
    71	Chosen: **`DECIMAL`**, and the reason is not exactness.
    72	
    73	On this data exactness does not distinguish them, and arguing from the general case would be
    74	arguing from a magnitude this source cannot produce. The decisive difference is **where a bad
    75	value fails**:
    76	
    77	| in the payload | `DECIMAL` contract | `DOUBLE` contract |
    78	|---|---|---|
    79	| `NaN` | `Conversion Error` at the cast, loudly, at `das unpack` | becomes `NaN`, propagates into a measure |
    80	| `Infinity` | same | becomes `Inf`, and a sum of it is `Inf` |
    81	
    82	A `NaN` discount through a `DOUBLE` contract produces a `NaN` revenue on one line, and a `NaN`
    83	anywhere in a sum makes the whole month `NaN` — in *both* answers alike, because both derive from
    84	the same landed value. So the acceptance check agrees, the gate is green, and a month's revenue is
    85	not a number. `DECIMAL` refuses the record at the door, which is where a contract is supposed to
    86	refuse things.
    87	
    88	That also stops the answer side depending on a coercion nobody wrote down. With `DECIMAL` in the
    89	contract the value is exact from the moment it lands, and the engine's widening to
    90	`DECIMAL(28,8)` is a widening rather than a rescue.
    91	
    92	### What this does not decide
    93	
    94	**Rounding is not decided here, and money is not rounded anywhere in this system.** Revenue
    95	carries every place the source's arithmetic produces, and the page formats for display without
    96	storing what it formatted. If a business ever needs revenue to two places, that is a *definition*
    97	— it belongs in `dab/model.yaml` with a sentence saying which way it rounds and why, and a check
    98	that verifies it. Rounding silently in a mapping would be exactly the "value somebody chose"
    99	ADR 0007 puts on the forbidden side of M5.
   100	
   101	## Consequences
   102	
   103	* Good, because a value the source should never have sent fails at the contract, once, rather
   104	  than becoming a `NaN` that both acceptance queries agree on
   105	* Good, because the exactness the acceptance check rests on is now ours from the landing zone
   106	  onward, not a vendor's silent coercion two layers later
   107	* Good, because it costs nothing measurable: two full builds, byte-identical DAR
   108	* Bad, because `DECIMAL(18, 4)` is **not** what the source declares, and §1.1 says DAS records
   109	  what the source sent. This is a knowing departure in the one direction §1.1 does not cover:
   110	  the vocabulary has no `REAL`, so recording it faithfully is not among the options
   111	* Bad, because a source value with more than four decimal places would now be refused rather than
   112	  approximated. That is the right failure and it is still a failure somebody has to handle
   113	
   114	## Confirmation
   115	
   116	`tests/test_das_sql.py` asserts the emitted expression in full, so the cast is there rather than a
   117	bare read and it carries the contract's declared precision and scale. That is **one** assertion in
   118	one file: this section previously cited `tests/test_contract.py` as a second, independent guard,
   119	and no such assertion exists there. Narrowing the one that does exist would have left the record
   120	claiming a guard that was never written.
   121	
   122	**A correction to the Consequences above, measured rather than reasoned.** They say a value with
   123	more than four decimal places "would now be refused rather than approximated". It is not:
   124	`cast('0.99999' AS DECIMAL(18, 4))` returns `1.0000` on DuckDB 1.5.5, with no error — a 99.999%
   125	discount recorded as 100%, which both of a question's answers would derive from the same rounded
   126	landed value and agree on. Only a `NaN`, an `Infinity`, or a value wider than eighteen digits
   127	fails at the cast. The decision stands and its reason stands — the `NaN` case is real and it was
   128	the one that mattered — but this type moves one silent failure rather than removing the class, and
   129	the register now says so too.
   130	
   131	The order-dependence witness is recorded in ADR 0007 and re-measured here on real values; nothing
   132	in the built system can now produce it, because no measure is a float at any layer — which is what
   133	the "both answers hold only exact values" check asserts on every build, per question.
   134	
   135	What is **not** confirmed: no test constructs a `NaN` payload and watches the contract refuse it.
   136	The behaviour was measured by hand against a scratch build and is written down here rather than
   137	pinned, because fabricating a payload the recorder never produced would be testing DuckDB's cast
   138	rather than this system's use of it. The property that matters — that a float never reaches an
   139	answer — is pinned, per question, on every build.

     2	status: accepted
     3	date: 2026-09-08
     4	decision-makers: [adss maintainers]
     5	slice: 4
     6	---
     7	
     8	# The bridge protects a measure and not the attribute it was made from, so a question may not aggregate a peripheral's number
     9	
    10	## Context and Problem Statement
    11	
    12	D-0001 puts every process into one shared `dar__uss`, departing from the blueprint's
    13	no-cross-dependency rule. Its entire justification, written in slice 1 and carried unexercised
    14	through three slices, is that *the fan trap R2 exists to prevent cannot occur in it* — because
    15	keys inherit along many-to-one edges and measures do not.
    16	
    17	Slice 4 is the first slice with two grains, so it is the first that can test that. It half holds.
    18	
    19	**The measures are safe, structurally, and this is the first demonstration of it.** Over the real
    20	two-grain bridge — 830 order rows and 2155 line rows — every shape returns the truth:
    21	
    22	| query | freight | revenue |
    23	|---|---|---|
    24	| both measures, whole bridge, no filter, no join | **64,942.69** ✓ | **1,265,793.0395** ✓ |
    25	| both, per order month, joined to `_calendar` (3794 rows) | **64,942.69** ✓ | **1,265,793.0395** ✓ |
    26	
    27	2155 line rows carry `order_key`, and freight does not move. That is what D-0001 has been
    28	asserting, and it is now a measurement.
    29	
    30	**The peripheral is not safe, and the query that breaks it is not exotic.** It is one join — the
    31	same join `q01` and `q02` already write:
    32	
    33	```sql
    34	SELECT sum(o.freight_charge)
    35	FROM dar__uss._bridge AS b
    36	INNER JOIN dar__uss."order" AS o ON b.order_key = o.order_key
    37	WHERE b._event = 'ordered';
    38	-- 207,306.10 against a true 64,942.69. Once per LINE.
    39	```
    40	
    41	`freight_charge` is a **published column of the order peripheral**. So the rule generalises to
    42	something D-0001 never said:
    43	
    44	> Any `NUMBER` attribute that is also a measure's source appears **twice** in `dar__uss` — once
    45	> as an additive measure on its owning stage, protected by a typed null on every other branch,
    46	> and once as a plain attribute on its peripheral, protected by nothing. `FREIGHT_CHARGE`,
    47	> `SHIP_LAG_DAYS` and `REVENUE` are all in that position.
    48	
    49	**And it was already live at slice 3, undetected.** On the warehouse as shipped in PR #3, before
    50	any line existed, the same query returns **128,897.71** against 64,942.69 — because `ORDER` had
    51	two events, so the bridge already had two rows per order. Slice 4 does not introduce the trap. It
    52	raises it from 1.98× to 3.19× and makes it reachable from another entity's stage, which is what a
    53	fan trap actually is.
    54	
    55	## Decision Drivers
    56	
    57	* the property D-0001 rests on is demonstrated or the deviation's argument is not carried
    58	* what the demonstration does *not* cover is stated, rather than left for a reader to discover
    59	* the trap is kept out of what this system publishes, since it cannot be kept out of SQL
    60	* nothing legitimate is removed to achieve it
    61	
    62	## Considered Options
    63	
    64	* Stop publishing a numeric attribute on a peripheral when it is also a measure's source
    65	* Publish it, and add a query-time rule to the bridge's contract
    66	* Publish it, add the rule, **and refuse a question that breaks it**
    67	
    68	## Decision Outcome
    69	
    70	Chosen: **the third.** The property is proved for measures, the limit of that proof is written
    71	into ADR 0002's contract as a third query-time rule, and a question whose answer query aggregates
    72	a peripheral's numeric column is **refused** by the question checker.
    73	
    74	**Why not remove the column.** A numeric attribute on a peripheral is legitimately useful — it is
    75	how a reader filters "orders whose freight was over 100" or sorts a table by it. Removing it to
    76	prevent a bad aggregate would break the good use to prevent the bad one, and would make the
    77	peripheral a worse description of the entity than the entity has.
    78	
    79	**Why a rule alone is not enough.** ADR 0002 already publishes two query-time rules and neither
    80	covers this one; a third would be true, unread and unenforced. This system's own position, stated
    81	in ADR 0006 and ADR 0008, is that a failure which is invisible gets refused where it can be seen.
    82	
    83	**What can actually be enforced.** Not "no reader writes a bad query" — a bridge does not stop a
    84	bad query, it makes the good one natural, and the honest form of that claim is narrower than it
    85	sounds. But every number this system *publishes* goes through a question's `uss.sql`, and those
    86	are files this repository owns and already checks. So: an answer query may not apply an aggregate
    87	to a column of a peripheral. It must aggregate `_measure__…` columns, which are the ones the
    88	bridge protects. That is checkable, it is checked, and it stops the trap entering the artefacts
    89	anybody reads.
    90	
    91	The rule has one deliberate hole: a question may still aggregate a peripheral's column if it does
    92	so outside `uss.sql`, and a person at a SQL prompt can do whatever they like. That is not a gap
    93	this decision can close and pretending otherwise would be the false comfort D-0001 has been
    94	running on.
    95	
    96	### D-0001 does not close
    97	
    98	Its exit condition, quoted whole, is: *"A second consumer needs isolation: a different shape of
    99	the same structure, or a group that must not see part of it."* That has not happened. Slice 4
   100	adds a fourth question read by one more persona, and a persona is not a consumer needing
   101	isolation — nothing here needs a different shape of the bridge and nothing must be hidden from
   102	anybody. Closing the entry now would be closing it for a reason that is not its own exit
   103	condition, which is how a register becomes decoration.
   104	
   105	What changes is the register's **Why**. It has said since slice 1 that the fan trap "cannot occur"
   106	in the shared structure. That is true of the measures and false of the peripherals, and the entry
   107	now says which, with the number.
   108	
   109	## Consequences
   110	
   111	* Good, because the argument D-0001 has been carried on for three slices is measured rather than
   112	  asserted, and the measurement is repeated on every build
   113	* Good, because the half that does *not* hold is written down with the query that breaks it and
   114	  the number it returns, rather than being discovered by somebody trusting the entry
   115	* Good, because the trap cannot enter a published answer, which is where it would be believed
   116	* Bad, because the refusal is a text rule over SQL, and a sufficiently determined query defeats
   117	  it — an aggregate spelled across a subquery, for instance. It raises the cost of the mistake
   118	  from zero to deliberate, which is what the other refusals in this system do too
   119	* Bad, because a question that genuinely wants a peripheral's number aggregated — "the largest
   120	  freight on any order" — now has to model it as a measure. That is more honest and more typing,
   121	  and it is the same trade ADR 0008 made
   122	
   123	## Confirmation
   124	
   125	`tests/test_fan_out.py` asserts the fan-out property directly, on the neutral fixture's two
   126	grains: a parent's measure summed over a bridge containing its children equals the parent's own
   127	total, the finer measure is right in the same scan, the coarser measure is null on every finer row
   128	while the inherited **key** is not, and — the falsifiable half — the parent's total does not move
   129	when a parent gains children. It runs the generated SQL against a warehouse it builds, rather than
   130	reading the SQL for substrings, because a substring assertion would pass a generator that emitted
   131	the right nulls in the wrong branch.
   132	
   133	That it can fail is measured rather than assumed. The generator was mutated so a measure inherits
   134	along an edge exactly as a key does — carried in the CTE that walks the edge, selected by the
   135	stage, and treated as the branch's own. It emits SQL DuckDB accepts, and the four assertions fail
   136	together: 402.00 in place of 150.75, three parent measures on the three child rows in place of
   137	none, and 904.50 against 402.00 when five children are added to a parent whose size did not
   138	change. A fifth test — the peripheral trap below — passes under that mutation, which is correct:
   139	the mutation is in the bridge and the trap is not.
   140	
   141	A generated data check, one per measure, asserts it is null on every row of every **event** that
   142	does not own it — the mechanism rather than the number, on the warehouse that was actually built.
   143	By event and not by stage: two events on one entity share a stage, so a per-stage check would let
   144	an order's shipment measure sit on its placement row and report nothing, and that is the likelier
   145	defect since every branch of the union comes off the same stage's CTE. `tests/test_measure_checks.py`
   146	runs each check against a bridge built to fail it, including that case.
   147	
   148	`tests/test_questions.py` asserts that an answer query aggregating a peripheral's column is
   149	refused, and that the same aggregate over a `_measure__` column is accepted. Every question in
   150	this repository is run through the refusal, so the rule is enforced rather than published.
   151	
   152	**It is not the text rule the Consequences above anticipated.** The refusal reads the engine's own
   153	parse tree for the answer query and the engine's own list of aggregate functions, so a `cast()`
   154	around the sum, a sum written as a window, a subquery, and an aggregate nobody thought to list are
   155	all caught — three of which a text rule would have missed, and the third is why the list is not
   156	kept by hand — and a ranking window is not one of them, because `row_number`, `rank`, `ntile`
   157	and `lag` are all in that list and refusing them blocked an ordinary answer with a reason that
   158	was not true. Seven mutations of the refusal have been run and all seven fail the suite,
   159	including refusing a ranking window again and reading only the first of an aggregate's
   160	columns — a peripheral multiplied into a measure is refused in either operand order.
   161	
   162	It is stricter than the trap requires, in two places worth naming. `count(*)` over the bridge is
   163	refused, because it counts measurement events rather than the thing asked about — two events on
   164	one entity and it doubles. And an aggregate over a `DISTINCT` peripheral column cannot be
   165	multiplied by a fan-out and is refused anyway: narrowing the rule to the aggregates that can
   166	actually be wrong would be a rule nobody could apply without already knowing which those are.
   167	
   168	**Where the rule actually lives, corrected.** The Decision Outcome above says the limit of the
   169	proof is "written into ADR 0002's contract as a third query-time rule". It is not, and under this
   170	repository's own rules it cannot be: a record is superseded, not edited. The rule is in
   171	[conventions §10](../conventions.md), which is the one convention document and the place a
   172	reviewer checks a question against, and in the `dar` and `adss` skills. ADR 0002's Confirmation
   173	points here. A reader following that sentence to ADR 0002 would have found nothing.
   174	
   175	**What defeats it, corrected.** This section previously claimed the rule was over-strict at the
   176	edge rather than porous there. That was wrong, and a security review found it: the refusal read
   177	the whole dotted reference, so a table aliased `_measure__x` laundered its own attributes through
   178	it — `sum(_measure__x.freight_charge)` was accepted, which is the exact aggregate this record
   179	exists to refuse, wearing a name it chose for itself. The refusal now decides on the last part of
   180	a reference, because what the bridge protects is a column, and an alias is the one part of a
   181	reference an author picks freely. A mutation restoring the old test fails the suite.
   182	
   183	One hole remains and is measured rather than assumed: a column aliased to a `_measure__` name
   184	inside a **subquery** — `sum(p._measure__pretend)` over `(SELECT freight_charge AS
   185	_measure__pretend …) AS p` — is still accepted. Closing it means resolving aliases through the
   186	parse tree rather than reading names, which is a larger piece of machinery than this decision
   187	warrants for a control that is already deliberate-only. It is recorded here rather than left for
   188	somebody to find, which is the difference between a limit and a defect.
   189	
   190	What is **not** confirmed: that no reader ever writes the bad query at a prompt. Nothing can
   191	confirm that, and the register now says so instead of implying otherwise.

=============== 0013
     1	---
     2	status: accepted
     3	date: 2026-09-08
     4	decision-makers: [adss maintainers]
     5	slice: 4
     6	---
     7	
     8	# An ingest is one observation, so every contract it lands shares one clock
     9	
    10	## Context and Problem Statement
    11	
    12	DAB's history is dated by when DAS observed the row. Northwind's `$metadata` has eleven entity
    13	types and about seventy properties and not one modified, updated or version column, so the
    14	observation time is the only history this platform can honestly claim — and `extracted_at` is
    15	`to_timestamp(cast(_dlt_load_id AS DOUBLE))`, the loader's own clock, so the partition key and the
    16	history clock derive from one fact rather than from two.
    17	
    18	**One fact per contract.** `land()` creates one pipeline per contract and `das ingest` runs them
    19	one after another, so a single ingest produces one `_dlt_load_id` per contract, each a fraction of
    20	a second after the last. Measured on a clean rebuild:
    21	
    22	| contract | `extracted_at` |
    23	|---|---|
    24	| `customers` | 06:40:43.517150 |
    25	| `order_details` | 06:40:43.916979 |
    26	| `orders` | 06:40:44.199092 |
    27	
    28	Contracts are landed in `sorted()` order, so `order_details` always precedes `orders`. Always: the
    29	underscore sorts before `s`, and the loader's id is the wall clock at `pipeline.run()`.
    30	
    31	Slice 4 is the first slice that reads one entity's history *as of another entity's observation*.
    32	ADR 0009 resolves an inherited date off the parent version in force when the child was observed:
    33	
    34	```sql
    35	LEFT JOIN dab."view_ORDER_hist" AS dated
    36	    ON dated."ORDER_key" = pair."ORDER_key"
    37	    AND dated.eff_tmstp <= revision._observed_at
    38	```
    39	
    40	`revision._observed_at` is `order_details.extracted_at`. `dated.eff_tmstp` is
    41	`orders.extracted_at`. They are 0.28 seconds apart, in the wrong direction, so **no ORDER version
    42	precedes any ORDER_LINE row**, the date resolves to null for every line, and ADR 0009's own rule —
    43	a row whose inherited date does not resolve gets no bridge row — removes all 2,155 of them. The
    44	`ordered` stage is empty and q04 returns nothing against the source's 23 rows.
    45	
    46	**It was green here for a reason that is not a reason.** This working tree's lake is gitignored
    47	and had accumulated: sixteen `orders` loads, twelve of them older than the earliest
    48	`order_details` load. `view_ORDER_hist` holds exactly one version, from the first of those, at
    49	22:11 the previous day — because `FULL_LOG` writes a new version only when the row changes, and
    50	the recording never changes. That single old version satisfies the `<=`, and it carries the same
    51	`PLACED_ON` any newer one would. A lake that accumulates across runs is a machine for turning a
    52	broken build green.
    53	
    54	The bug is not the `<=`. ADR 0006 and ADR 0009 are right that the parent must be resolved as of
    55	the child's observation. The bug is that "the observation" is not one time.
    56	
    57	## Decision Drivers
    58	
    59	* an as-of join between two entities must not depend on the order their contracts were landed in
    60	* the fix belongs where the fact is wrong, not where the fact is read
    61	* DAS may not learn what DAB's relationships are; the flow runs one way
    62	* what a clean clone builds is what the repository claims, or the claim is worthless
    63	
    64	## Considered Options
    65	
    66	* **One clock per ingest** — every contract landed by one `adss das ingest` gets one `extracted_at`
    67	* **Land contracts in dependency order** — sort parents before children
    68	* **Fall back to the parent's earliest version** when none precedes the child
    69	* **Compare dates rather than instants** in the as-of join
    70	
    71	## Decision Outcome
    72	
    73	Chosen: **one clock per ingest.** `das ingest` takes the time once and every contract it lands
    74	carries it, so `extracted_at` says when the *system* observed the source rather than when a
    75	particular pipeline happened to start. `<=` is then satisfied by equality and the as-of join is
    76	independent of landing order.
    77	
    78	This is a decision about meaning, not a workaround. Rows fetched by one run of one command are one
    79	observation of one source. Dating them individually says the business changed between two HTTP
    80	calls, which nothing here can know and nothing downstream should have to reason about.
    81	
    82	`extracted_at` becomes an explicit column landed beside the payload, rather than a derivation from
    83	`_dlt_load_id`. That is the same number of clocks the spike argued for — "record the source once;
    84	one fact, in two shapes, never two clocks" — restored. What exists today is three clocks, one per
    85	contract, which the spike's own rule already forbade and nobody noticed because nothing compared
    86	them until now.
    87	
    88	**Why not land in dependency order.** It would fix the direction and not the cause: two contracts
    89	would still carry two times, so a partial ingest, a retry, or any future check comparing
    90	observation times across entities would break the same way. It also requires DAS to know which
    91	entity is a parent of which, and that is DAB's knowledge — the layer whose whole purpose is to be
    92	independent of where the data came from would have to be consulted by the layer that fetches it.
    93	That is the flow rule, backwards, to fix a clock.
    94	
    95	**Why not fall back to the earliest version.** It changes what "as of" means, so a parent this
    96	system genuinely had not yet observed would be resolved against a version from its future. It also
    97	fixes one query rather than the fact, and the next as-of comparison would need the same patch.
    98	
    99	**Why not compare dates.** A load spanning midnight breaks it, and the answer to "these two
   100	instants are wrongly ordered" is not "look at them less closely".
   101	
   102	### What this does not change
   103	
   104	`extracted_on`, the hive partition key, is still the loader's own date, and the existing clock
   105	check still asserts it equals `cast(extracted_at AS DATE)` in UTC. The two can now disagree only
   106	if a load starts before midnight and writes after it, which is the case that check was written for.
   107	
   108	## Consequences
   109	
   110	* Good, because an as-of join between two entities means what it says, and does not depend on the
   111	  alphabetical order of contract file names
   112	* Good, because a clean clone builds what this repository claims it builds — which was not true of
   113	  slice 4 as first committed
   114	* Good, because the rule generalises: every future comparison of observation times across entities
   115	  is now comparing one fact to itself
   116	* Bad, because two contracts landed by two separate commands still carry two times, correctly —
   117	  they are two observations — so a reader who splits an ingest gets history that says so. That is
   118	  the honest answer and it is still a surprise waiting for somebody
   119	* Bad, because `extracted_at` is now a column this layer writes rather than one it derives, so a
   120	  source field named `extracted_at` is refused where before it was merely shadowed. It was already
   121	  reserved, so nothing changes in practice
   122	* Bad, because the local lake that hid this is still there and still accumulates. Nothing here
   123	  makes a stale lake fail; CI's clean checkout is what says the build is real
   124	
   125	## Confirmation
   126	
   127	`tests/test_das_round_trip.py` lands two contracts in one ingest, in the order that broke this —
   128	the child's contract first — and asserts every row of both carries the same `extracted_at`, and
   129	that the second landed is not later than the first. It fails on the previous derivation.
   130	
   131	The measurement above is repeatable: a clean tree with no `das/lake/` builds an empty `ordered`
   132	stage before this change and 2,155 rows after it, and `adss check` reports `q04: the source and the
   133	star schema agree` in the second case only. CI does exactly that on every push — checkout, build,
   134	check — with no lake, so the clean rebuild is the standing test rather than something anybody has
   135	to remember to run.
   136	
   137	**A correction to the Consequences above, which were written before the code.** They say nothing
   138	here makes a stale lake fail. Building it showed otherwise, twice over. A load landed before this
   139	change has no `extracted_at` column at all, `union_by_name` reads it back as null, and DAB then
   140	historizes on a null clock — which surfaced as three duplicate-version findings naming FULL
   141	ingestion, a cause that had nothing to do with it. Worse, the clock check passed on those rows:
   142	it said `extracted_on <> cast(extracted_at AS DATE)`, and a null is neither equal nor unequal to
   143	anything, so it counted neither side of exactly the rows it exists to find. It says `IS DISTINCT
   144	FROM` now, `tests/test_das_executes.py` lands a load with no clock and asserts the check finds it,
   145	and a stale lake therefore fails on its own layer with its own name rather than three layers later
   146	under somebody else's.
   147	
   148	The remedy for a stale lake is to delete it. `.gitignore` already says everything in it is
   149	reproducible from `das/fixtures`, and it is: the local lake was removed and rebuilt, 48 checks.
   150	
   151	What is **not** confirmed: that no other pair of facts in this system is compared across two
   152	clocks. This one was found by a question failing, not by a check that looks for the shape.

   200	    raising, so the built table stops matching the published contract. The glossary half is

   202	    references resolve against and what the page renders. A reader would be shown a plausible
   203	    sentence about the wrong number, and everything would pass.

   206	    for event in uss.events:

   211	                    f"{event.entity_id} declares {measure.id} on both {seen[key]} and "
   212	                    f"{event.id}. A measure is named for its entity and owned by its event, so "
   213	                    f"the two would share one column -- and {event.id}'s definition would "
   214	                    f"replace {seen[key]}'s in the glossary, which nothing checks and the page "
   215	                    f"renders. Give them separate ids, or one definition covering both."
   216	                )

   270	def _version_cte(model: Model, event: Event) -> str:
   271	    """The version of each entity this event is measured on: the latest in which it is dated."""
   272	    entity = model.entity(event.entity_id)
   273	    inherited, attribute_id = event.dated_by
   274	    date = crossing(attribute_id)
   275	    held = "revision"
   276	    lines = [
   277	        f"    {held}.{crossing(entity.source_key)} AS {entity.key_column}",
   278	        f"    {held}.eff_tmstp AS _observed_at",
   279	    ]
   280	    # An inherited date is resolved with the key, in the CTE that walks the edge, so both are
   281	    # true as of one instant. ADR 0009.
   282	    if inherited is None:
   283	        lines.append(f"    cast({held}.{date} AS DATE) AS _event_date")
   284	    for measure in event.measures:
   285	        column = f"_measure__{entity.object_name}__{measure.id.lower()}"
   286	        if measure.aggregate is Aggregate.COUNT:
   287	            value = f"cast(1 AS {COUNT_TYPE})"
   288	        else:
   289	            attribute = crossing(str(measure.attribute_id))
   290	            value = f"cast({held}.{attribute} AS {SUM_TYPE})"
   291	        lines.append(f"    {value} AS {column}")
   292	    selected = ",\n".join(lines)
   293	    # An inherited date is filtered where it is resolved, not here: this entity has no such
   294	    # column to filter on.
   295	    dated = "" if inherited else f"WHERE {held}.{date} IS NOT NULL\n"
   296	    return (
   297	        f"{event.name}__version AS (\n"
   298	        f"SELECT\n{selected}\n"
   299	        f'FROM dab."view_{entity.id}_hist" AS {held}\n'
   300	        f"{dated}"
   301	        f"QUALIFY row_number() OVER (\n"
   302	        f"    PARTITION BY {held}.{crossing(entity.source_key)}\n"
   303	        f"    ORDER BY {held}.eff_tmstp DESC\n"
   304	        f") = 1\n"
   305	        f")"
   306	    )

   309	def _inherit_cte(model: Model, event: Event, edge: Relationship) -> str:
   310	    """One inherited key: the pair in force when the inheriting row was observed. ADR 0006.
   311	
   312	    Resolved per inheriting ROW rather than per key -- the partition carries the observation
   313	    time -- because that is the whole reason ADR 0006 chose the observation time over "now".
   314	    A stage that kept more than the latest version of an entity would otherwise hand every one
   315	    of those versions the same parent, which is "as of now" wearing the other rule's clothes.
   316	
   317	    Read from `v_<SRC>_<NAME>_<TGT>`, which is the raw pairs plus the relationship's name, and
   318	    ranked here rather than by the engine. The engine's own ranked view answers a different
   319	    question -- who the parent is *now* -- and answers it with `rank()`, which returns two rows
   320	    for a child whose source named two parents at one instant. Two rows here would double that
   321	    child's measures, so the ranking is `row_number()` and the tie is refused by a data check.
   322	    """
   323	    source = model.entity(edge.source_entity_id)
   324	    target = model.entity(edge.target_entity_id)
   325	    held = edge.id.lower()
   326	    # If the event is dated by this target's attribute, the date is resolved here, off the same
   327	    # parent the key came from, so both are true as of one instant. ADR 0009.
   328	    inherited, attribute_id = event.dated_by
   329	    dates = inherited == target.id
   330	    carried = f",\n    cast(dated.{crossing(attribute_id)} AS DATE) AS _event_date" if dates else ""
   331	    # The candidate versions are the DATED ones. Without that clause the latest version wins
   332	    # even when it is the one that blanked the date -- an ordinary shape in a full change log --
   333	    # and the child's date is null, so ADR 0009's own rule removes its row. A whole grain then
   334	    # leaves the bridge while the parent's own event stays dated, and nothing says so.
   335	    joined = (
   336	        f'\nLEFT JOIN dab."view_{target.id}_hist" AS dated\n'
   337	        f"    ON dated.{crossing(target.source_key)} = pair.{crossing(target.source_key)}\n"
   338	        f"    AND dated.{crossing(attribute_id)} IS NOT NULL\n"
   339	        f"    AND dated.eff_tmstp <= revision._observed_at"
   340	        if dates
   341	        else ""
   342	    )
   343	    return (
   344	        f"{event.name}__{held} AS (\n"
   345	        f"SELECT\n"
   346	        f"    revision.{source.key_column} AS {source.key_column},\n"
   347	        f"    revision._observed_at AS _observed_at,\n"
   348	        f"    pair.{crossing(target.source_key)} AS {target.key_column}"
   349	        f"{carried}\n"
   350	        f"FROM {event.name}__version AS revision\n"
   351	        f'LEFT JOIN dab."v_{edge.id}" AS pair\n'
   352	        f"    ON pair.{crossing(source.source_key)} = revision.{source.key_column}\n"
   353	        f"    AND pair.rel_name = '{edge.id}'\n"
   354	        f"    AND pair.row_st = 'Y'\n"
   355	        f"    AND pair.eff_tmstp <= revision._observed_at"
   356	        f"{joined}\n"
   357	        f"QUALIFY row_number() OVER (\n"
   358	        f"    PARTITION BY revision.{source.key_column}, revision._observed_at\n"
   359	        f"    ORDER BY\n"
   360	        f"        pair.eff_tmstp DESC,\n"
   361	        f"        pair.ver_tmstp DESC,\n"
   362	        f"        pair.{crossing(target.source_key)}"
   363	        + (",\n        dated.eff_tmstp DESC" if dates else "")
   364	        + "\n) = 1\n"
   365	        ")"
   366	    )

   369	def _stage_cte(model: Model, event: Event) -> str:
   370	    """One stage: the entity's version, with the key of everything it inherits from."""
   371	    entity = model.entity(event.entity_id)
   372	    edges = model.edges_from(entity.id)
   373	    inherited, _ = event.dated_by
   374	    dater = "revision"
   375	    if inherited is not None:
   376	        dater = next(edge.id.lower() for edge in edges if edge.target_entity_id == inherited)
   377	    lines = [
   378	        f"    revision.{entity.key_column} AS {entity.key_column}",
   379	        "    revision._observed_at AS _observed_at",
   380	        f"    {dater}._event_date AS _event_date",
   381	    ]
   382	    lines += [
   383	        f"    {edge.id.lower()}.{model.entity(edge.target_entity_id).key_column} "
   384	        f"AS {model.entity(edge.target_entity_id).key_column}"
   385	        for edge in edges
   386	    ]
   387	    lines += [
   388	        f"    revision._measure__{entity.object_name}__{measure.id.lower()} "
   389	        f"AS _measure__{entity.object_name}__{measure.id.lower()}"
   390	        for measure in event.measures
   391	    ]
   392	    # One row per inheriting row in each of these, so none of the joins can fan out. LEFT
   393	    # anyway: the row that inherits nothing is kept by the join inside the CTE, and an inner
   394	    # join here would undo that one level up.
   395	    joins = "".join(
   396	        f"\nLEFT JOIN {event.name}__{edge.id.lower()} AS {edge.id.lower()}\n"
   397	        f"    ON {edge.id.lower()}.{entity.key_column} = revision.{entity.key_column}\n"
   398	        f"    AND {edge.id.lower()}._observed_at = revision._observed_at"
   399	        for edge in edges
   400	    )
   401	    selected = ",\n".join(lines)
   402	    # An event's own date is filtered in the version CTE; an inherited one is not there to
   403	    # filter, so it is filtered where it was resolved. Same rule, one step along the walk: a
   404	    # row whose date does not resolve is absent rather than dated null -- and the calendar's
   405	    # inner join would otherwise drop it silently, which looks like the rule working. ADR 0009.
   406	    absent = "" if inherited is None else f"\nWHERE {dater}._event_date IS NOT NULL"
   407	    return (
   408	        f"{event.name} AS (\nSELECT\n{selected}\n"
   409	        f"FROM {event.name}__version AS revision{joins}{absent}\n)"
   410	    )

   413	def _branch(model: Model, uss: Uss, event: Event, keys: tuple[str, ...]) -> str:
   414	    """One branch of the union: this stage's own columns, and a typed NULL for the rest."""
   415	    entity = model.entity(event.entity_id)
   416	    carried = {entity.key_column} | {
   417	        model.entity(edge.target_entity_id).key_column for edge in model.edges_from(entity.id)
   418	    }
   419	    lines = [
   420	        f"    '{entity.object_name}' AS _stage",
   421	        f"    '{event.name}' AS _event",
   422	        f"    {event.name}._event_date AS _event_date",
   423	        "    TRUE AS _is_current",
   424	        f"    {event.name}._observed_at AS _observed_at",
   425	    ]
   426	    for key in keys:
   427	        value = f"{event.name}.{key}" if key in carried else "cast(NULL AS VARCHAR)"
   428	        lines.append(f"    {value} AS {key}")
   429	    owned = {column for candidate, _, column in uss.measure_columns() if candidate is event}
   430	    for _, measure, column in uss.measure_columns():
   431	        value = f"{event.name}.{column}" if column in owned else f"cast(NULL AS {measure.sql_type})"
   432	        lines.append(f"    {value} AS {column}")
   433	    return "SELECT\n" + ",\n".join(lines) + f"\nFROM {event.name} AS {event.name}"

   436	def entity_ids(model: Model, uss: Uss) -> tuple[str, ...]:
   437	    """Every entity the bridge names, in MODEL order: the ones with events, and the ones they
   438	    inherit from. An entity reached only by inheritance still needs a peripheral, or the bridge
   439	    carries a key that joins to nothing.
   440	    """
   441	    touched = {event.entity_id for event in uss.events}
   442	    touched |= {
   443	        edge.target_entity_id for event in uss.events for edge in model.edges_from(event.entity_id)
   444	    }
   445	    return tuple(entity.id for entity in model.entities if entity.id in touched)

   448	def entity_keys(model: Model, uss: Uss) -> tuple[str, ...]:
   449	    """One key column per entity the bridge names, in MODEL order.
   450	
   451	    Model order, not event order: reordering two events in the sidecar is not a model change,
   452	    and it must not rearrange a contract that consumers are written against. The check cannot
   453	    catch that on its own, because it derives what it expects from this same function.
   454	    """
   455	    return tuple(model.entity(entity_id).key_column for entity_id in entity_ids(model, uss))

   458	def bridge_columns(model: Model, uss: Uss) -> tuple[str, ...]:
   459	    """The published column contract, in order.
   460	
   461	    Grouped: the structural columns, then one key per entity in model order, then one column
   462	    per measure in declaration order.
   463	
   464	    That grouping means the contract does NOT only ever grow at the end, and saying otherwise
   465	    would be the more comfortable lie. A new entity appends a key, and because keys precede
   466	    measures, every measure column moves right. An entity inserted in the middle of the model
   467	    moves the keys after it as well. So the model file's own order is part of this contract,
   468	    and nothing here can catch a rearrangement: the check that compares the built bridge to
   469	    this contract derives what it expects from this same function, so both sides move together
   470	    and it passes either way.

470	    and it passes either way.
   471	
   472	    What makes that tolerable rather than a defect is that nothing reads this table by
   473	    position. Conventions section 3 forbids `SELECT *`, the questions name their columns and
   474	    so does the destination. A consumer that did read positionally would be reading a contract
   475	    this docstring does not offer it. New entities still go at the end, because moving a key
   476	    column is a bigger change than moving a measure. Blueprint B7.
   477	    """
   478	    keys = entity_keys(model, uss)
   479	    structural = ("_stage", "_event", "_event_date", "_is_current", "_observed_at")
   480	    return structural + keys + tuple(column for _, _, column in uss.measure_columns())

   483	def bridge_sql(model: Model, uss: Uss) -> str:
   484	    """One row per measurement event, over every stage the declarations name."""
   485	    keys = entity_keys(model, uss)
   486	    ctes = ",\n\n".join(
   487	        cte
   488	        for event in uss.events
   489	        for cte in (
   490	            _version_cte(model, event),
   491	            *(_inherit_cte(model, event, edge) for edge in model.edges_from(event.entity_id)),
   492	            _stage_cte(model, event),
   493	        )
   494	    )
   495	    branches = "\n\nUNION ALL\n\n".join(_branch(model, uss, event, keys) for event in uss.events)
   496	    return f"{_GENERATED}\nCREATE OR REPLACE TABLE {BRIDGE.sql} AS\nWITH {ctes}\n\n{branches};\n"

   521	def calendar_sql() -> str:
   522	    """Dense and daily across everything the bridge holds. Civil arithmetic only.
   523	
   524	    A calendar containing only the days something happened is not a calendar: a month with
   525	    no events must still appear in a time series. Fiscal periods and holidays are business
   526	    meaning and would need a definition, so they belong in the model, not in a generator.
   527	    """
   528	    return (
   529	        f"{_GENERATED}\n"
   530	        f"CREATE OR REPLACE TABLE {CALENDAR.sql} AS\n"
   531	        f"WITH bounds AS (\n"
   532	        f"SELECT\n"
   533	        f"    min(b._event_date) AS first_date,\n"
   534	        f"    max(b._event_date) AS last_date\n"
   535	        f"FROM {BRIDGE.sql} AS b\n"
   536	        f"),\n\n"
   537	        f"every_day AS (\n"
   538	        f"SELECT\n"
   539	        f"    cast(d.day AS DATE) AS date_key\n"
   540	        f"FROM bounds AS bo\n"
   541	        f"CROSS JOIN range(\n"
   542	        f"    bo.first_date, bo.last_date + INTERVAL 1 DAY, INTERVAL 1 DAY\n"
   543	        f") AS d (day)\n"
   544	        f")\n\n"
   545	        f"SELECT\n"
   546	        f"    d.date_key AS date_key,\n"
   547	        f"    cast(year(d.date_key) AS INTEGER) AS year_number,\n"
   548	        f"    cast(quarter(d.date_key) AS INTEGER) AS quarter_of_year,\n"
   549	        f"    cast(month(d.date_key) AS INTEGER) AS month_of_year,\n"
   550	        f"    cast(day(d.date_key) AS INTEGER) AS day_of_month,\n"
   551	        f"    cast(date_trunc('year', d.date_key) AS DATE) AS year_start,\n"
   552	        f"    cast(date_trunc('quarter', d.date_key) AS DATE) AS quarter_start,\n"
   553	        f"    cast(date_trunc('month', d.date_key) AS DATE) AS month_start,\n"
   554	        f"    strftime(d.date_key, '%Y') || '-Q' || cast(quarter(d.date_key) AS VARCHAR) "
   555	        f"AS quarter_label,\n"
   556	        f"    strftime(d.date_key, '%Y-%m') AS month_label\n"
   557	        f"FROM every_day AS d;\n"
   558	    )

   561	def definitions(model: Model, uss: Uss) -> dict[str, str]:
   562	    """Every definition, by the token that refers to it. Copied verbatim, never composed.
   563	
   564	    A generator that composed a definition would be a third place the data is explained,
   565	    and the worst kind: one nobody wrote and nobody reviews.
   566	    """
   567	    found = dict(model.definitions())
   568	    for event in uss.events:
   569	        found[f"{event.entity_id}.events.{event.id}"] = event.definition
   570	        for measure in event.measures:
   571	            found[f"{event.entity_id}.measures.{measure.id}"] = measure.definition
   572	    return found

   260	def relationship_checks(model: Model) -> dict[str, str]:

   262	
   263	    All three failures look identical in the built warehouse -- an inherited key that is null,
   264	    or wrong, on rows that look like data rather than like a defect -- and none of them is
   265	    reported by the engine at deploy, at execute, or by a question's acceptance queries.
   266	    """

   268	    for edge in model.relationships:
   269	        source = model.entity(edge.source_entity_id)
   270	        target = model.entity(edge.target_entity_id)
   271	        pairs = f'dab."v_{edge.id}"'
   272	        open_pairs = (
   273	            f"FROM {pairs} AS pair\nWHERE pair.rel_name = '{edge.id}'\n    AND pair.row_st = 'Y'"
   274	        )
   275	        name = edge.id.lower()
   276	
   277	        # The generator resolves a tie with row_number(), so it can never fan out -- but
   278	        # resolving a tie deterministically is still choosing arbitrarily between two answers.
   279	        generated[f"{name}__one_target"] = (
   280	            f"{_EDGE}\n"
   281	            f"SELECT count(*) AS ambiguities\n"
   282	            f"FROM (\n"
   283	            f"    SELECT\n"
   284	            f"        pair.{crossing(source.source_key)} AS source_key,\n"
   285	            f"        pair.eff_tmstp AS observed_at\n"
   286	            f"    {open_pairs}\n"
   287	            f"    GROUP BY pair.{crossing(source.source_key)}, pair.eff_tmstp\n"
   288	            f"    HAVING count(DISTINCT pair.{crossing(target.source_key)}) > 1\n"

   294	        generated[f"{name}__loaded"] = (

   297	            f"FROM (SELECT 1 AS declared) AS edge\n"
   298	            f"WHERE NOT EXISTS (\n"
   299	            f"    SELECT 1\n"

   302	        )

   152	    'A12' + '3' into one key -- is review-only until there is a composite key to check.

   209	def reaching(expression: str) -> bool:
   210	    """Whether an expression leaves the row it is written on. M5.
   211	
   212	    Arithmetic and same-row functions do not, however they are spelled; a subquery, a join, a
   213	    window or an aggregate does.
   214	    """
   215	    return bool(
   216	        _REACHING.search(_without_keyword_from(expression)) or _AGGREGATE.search(expression)
   217	    )

   219	
   220	def _without_keyword_from(expression: str) -> str:
   221	    """The expression with the syntactic FROM of each such function blanked, and nothing else.
   222	
   223	    Only that one token, and only when it is genuinely inside the call. An earlier version
   224	    discarded the whole argument list, which excused the very thing M5 exists to stop: a
   225	    subquery hidden in `extract(DAY FROM (SELECT ...))` became invisible. Taking simply the
   226	    next FROM instead was no better -- in `trim(a) FROM elsewhere` the next one is the reach.
   227	
   228	    So the scan finds the first FROM at the call's own bracket depth, and gives up at the
   229	    bracket that closes the call. It steps over single-quoted text, because a bracket inside a
   230	    string literal is not a bracket, and a scan that believed otherwise would run off the end
   231	    and hand the checker half an expression to judge.
   232	    """
   233	    out = expression
   234	    for call in _KEYWORD_FROM.finditer(expression):
   235	        found = _syntactic_from(out, call.end())
   236	        if found is not None:
   237	            out = out[:found] + " " * 4 + out[found + 4 :]
   238	    return out
